variants.name: record + List.copyOf compact constructor
variants.idiom_name: record + List.copyOf/Map.copyOf in a compact constructor + withers
variants.implementation_notes: Java 16 records make the immutable carrier a language feature - components become private final fields with generated accessors and content equality - and the Java 10 copyOf factories (List.copyOf, Set.copyOf, Map.copyOf) produce genuinely unmodifiable collections, so a compact constructor that copies its collection components replaces hand-written defensive copies in both directions. An update is a wither returning a new record, and for large nested data a persistent collection library supplies structural sharing instead of copies. The classic form (final fields, private constructor, static factories, Collections.unmodifiableX) is still needed before Java 16, and unmodifiableX remains a live view that must wrap a private copy or callers will still observe changes made through the original reference.
pitfalls: Records are shallowly immutable: a component of a mutable type (List, Date, array) is shared unless copied in the compact constructor or replaced by an immutable type (Instant, List.copyOf).
List.copyOf, Set.copyOf and Map.copyOf reject nulls with NullPointerException, so nullable elements need an explicit policy before copying.
Safe publication is a separate concern: only final fields get the Java Memory Model guarantee, so a non-final reference must be published through volatile, AtomicReference or another safe mechanism.

variants.name: final fields + Collections.unmodifiableX (Java 8 classic)
variants.idiom_name: final fields + private constructor/static factory + Collections.unmodifiableX over private copies
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-record classic: final fields, a private constructor or static factory, defensive copies in both directions and Collections.unmodifiableX as the read-only view. Use it when the source level is Java 8-15, when the type must stay a class (instance methods, serialization hooks, API compatibility) or when the value must implement interfaces that records cannot extend. The copy-in/copy-out discipline is exactly what records and copyOf mechanise later, so this variant is the migration source as well as the fallback.
pitfalls: Collections.unmodifiableX is a view, not a copy: wrap a private copy or mutations through the original collection stay visible to holders.
Make the class final or hide it behind an interface: a subclass that adds mutable state silently voids the guarantee for code holding the base type.
JavaBeans-style frameworks need a no-argument constructor and setters, so map to a mutable DTO at the boundary instead of weakening the type.

variants.name: Vavr persistent collections
variants.idiom_name: Vavr List/Map/Set with structural sharing (plus/put return new collections)
variants.implementation_notes: Vavr's persistent List, Map and Set keep updates functional: plus, put and remove return a new collection that shares structure with the old one, so a large nested value can be updated in logarithmic time instead of being deep-copied. Choose it where versions of big structures stay alive - caches, undo stacks, event-sourced state, editors - or where copying dominates the profile; the trade is a third-party dependency and a collection API that is not java.util, so conversions happen at the boundary.
pitfalls: Vavr collections are not java.util collections: convert at API boundaries (toJavaList) and budget for the dependency.
Structural sharing keeps old versions alive through shared nodes; retain only the versions you actually need or the history becomes a memory leak.
Mixed collections (JDK List plus Vavr List in one type) force conversions and invite accidental copies - pick one representation per value.
